question: What limits the forecast, the kind of model or the information in its inputs? 1, 2 and 3 days ahead.
headline: Among the models tried, the limit is the information in the inputs, not the network: 1 day ahead, on the same inputs (past weather + river gauge) four kinds of model lie within 0.03 NSE and 8 percentage points of onsets warned of each other, while rain up to the evening of the issue day lifts the LSTM's onsets warned from 19% to 30% (about a quarter of the gap; in NSE the result is mixed) and rain up to midnight from a radar- and gauge-anchored analysis (AORC, an analysis made after the fact) lifts them from 19% to 51% (48% with the real-time radar product Stage IV in its place); 2 and 3 days ahead a real weather forecast (GEFS) lifts them from 8% and 6% to 39% and 37% (in NSE the gain is mixed); a perfect weather forecast, an upper bound that cannot be had in practice, would give 64% 1 day ahead and 67% and 68% 2 and 3 days ahead; for onsets the verdict is still NOT YET for every set that could be had in practice.

how_to_read.levels: The six sets of information of the upper block, from top to bottom, for the drawn lead time (1 day). lstm: the forecast averaged over the seeds (nse = median NSE of the basins; onset_warned and onset_false = share of the onsets warned and share of the onset warnings that were false, at the high-flow level itself; onset_verdict by 'criteria' at that level, onset_verdict_at_chosen_level as the results files store it for the level chosen on the validation years; *_seeds = the single seeds, in the order of 'seeds'). others: the other kinds of model (drawn = it is in the figure; same_inputs = it reads the same information as the LSTM of that set; against_lstm = the comparison stored in the results file, read by the rule of section 4.2 of the report). real_time (set wqa): the check with Stage IV radar in place of AORC. control_not_drawn (set wqa): the same AORC rain over the rain table's own window.
how_to_read.far: The lower block: the five sets of 2 days ahead (far.l2) and 3 days ahead (far.l3), each as in 'levels' (lstm, others), and 'steps': the gain of each set over the rain table + river gauge, and the forecast's own part (forecast_over_rain_to_midnight), with the reading of section 4.2 (nse_reading: clear / mixed / none / loss).
how_to_read.steps: LSTM of one set minus LSTM of another, differences taken before rounding; onset_warned_points in percentage points. aorc_over_rain_table and rain_up_to_evening are the gains over past weather + river gauge that the bars of the figure show, and perfect_forecast the whole gap. spread_between_model_kinds: highest minus lowest of the models on the same inputs (wq is the bracket of the figure; w and wqa are not drawn).
how_to_read.finding: Whether the numbers show what the title says, and the rule: holds = on the same inputs (past weather + river gauge) the kinds of model lie closer together than every step of the LSTM to the right of them, in onsets warned and in NSE. The title, the subtitle and the headline state the finding only when it holds.
how_to_read.verdicts: The verdict for onsets of every set the figure draws, at the fixed level and at the level chosen on the validation years; practice.all_not_yet is the sentence of the headline.
how_to_read.n_onsets: Onsets of the test years by lead time, the basins counted together; the drawn share is of l1 above and of l2 and l3 below.
how_to_read.not_drawn: The quantities of the upper block's sets at 2 and 3 days (l2, l3); the sets that the lower block draws are also in 'far'.
how_to_read.forecast_1_day: The real forecast and the perfect rain substituted in the same way at 1 day, which the figure does not draw (the forecast warns of fewer onsets at the fixed level there, with fewer false warnings).
how_to_read.extras: Numbers of the experiments of 7 and 8 October that the figure does not draw, named in the notes: ERA5 rain to midnight, 63 training rivers, the forecast retrained on its own split.
how_to_read.files: Three renderings of the one drawing, made by the same function from this file: report = with its own title, subtitle and footnote; plain = the same drawing without them and without the rows 'river gauge only' and 'past weather only' (page 1 of the report, where the caption carries the words and the page holds one figure of this height; see figure.plain); talk = for the closing slide, larger lettering, without the rows and small marks that are not in the headline. figure.renderings holds the size and the lettering of each, and what it leaves out.
how_to_read.sources: For every number: the ONE file and key it was read from (or how it was computed here), and the other places that hold the same quantity and were checked against it. in_figure: the number is plotted or printed in the figure; file_id and key let the check at the end of the build read it again.

finding.rule: holds when, on the same inputs (past weather + river gauge), highest minus lowest of the kinds of model is smaller than every step of the LSTM to the right of them (rain up to the evening; the AORC rain up to midnight beyond it; what is left of the gap to the perfect weather forecast, an upper bound), in onsets warned AND in NSE

notes: Test years 2005-2014, 12 basins. The upper block of the figure is 1 day ahead, the lower block two and three days ahead. Onsets warned: the share of the onsets of the test years (611, 951 and 1,116 at 1, 2 and 3 days) for which a warning was given, the 12 basins counted together, at the high-flow level itself. NSE: the median of the 12 basins (1 is a perfect forecast). The verdict table of the report (section 5) counts warnings at the level chosen on the validation years instead: 1 day ahead that is the high-flow level itself for past weather + river gauge and the perfect weather forecast (the upper bound), and 0.95 times that level for past weather only, where the LSTM warns of 19% of the onsets (in the figure: 17%).

An onset is a high-flow day forecast while the river was still at or below the high-flow level (the level exceeded on 5% of the days of the training years): the warning that matters, because the river is not yet high when it is issued.

The perfect weather forecast (hatched) is an upper bound that cannot be had in practice: the LSTM reads the weather recorded for the days being forecast. A real weather forecast has errors, so a real system lands below it: the real forecast of the lower block (GEFS) is one measurement of where, 39% and 37% of the onsets 2 and 3 days ahead against 67% and 68% for the perfect weather. Even with the perfect weather the LSTM warns of 64% of the onsets 1 day ahead, below the 70% that GO asks for. The bound is that of this LSTM, not of every kind of model: given a perfect weather forecast, the ridge regression warns of 73% of the onsets, with 59% of its onset warnings false (the LSTM: 26% false; GO allows at most 30%). The simple models are not drawn there, because they do not read the same days of weather as the LSTM 1 day ahead. The lower block has a second upper bound, the perfect rain of the three days (the AORC rain of the three days being forecast, an analysis made after the fact, nothing else, beside the rain up to midnight): 69% and 71% of the onsets.

AORC (the set '+ rain up to midnight, radar- and gauge-anchored') is an analysis made after the fact: hourly rain at 1 km anchored on gauges and radar, corrected about 10 days after the hour, and before 2002, which are all the training years, disaggregated daily totals (results/aorc_rain_to_midnight.json). It says what well-measured rain up to midnight is worth, not what a service reads at midnight. The real-time check (hollow diamonds; results/stage4_realtime.json): the three saved networks of that set, given Stage IV radar and gauge rain (the product a service at midnight would read) in place of AORC on the issue day of each of the 611 onsets, warn of 294 (48%) against 313 (51%) with AORC and 114 (19%) with the rain table alone: 90% of the AORC effect survives (95% interval 85% to 97%); with the last hour of the issue day left out, as the delay of a real-time product would, 275 (45%). The networks were trained on AORC, not on Stage IV, and the false warnings were not tested on days without an onset.

The control of the rain-timing experiment (the hollow circle) is the same rain one day older: still a second rain product, but with no rain later than the rain table's own. It warns of 19% of the onsets (median NSE 0.60), against 19% (0.59) without the extra rain and 30% (0.67) with the rain up to the evening: in onsets warned the gain is the rain of the issue day, not the second rain product (every single seed with that rain is above every seed without it and every seed of the control).

The control of the AORC set (not drawn) is the same AORC rain over the rain table's own window, 09:00 to 09:00, with no new hour: it warns of 18% of the onsets (median NSE 0.55), against 19% (0.59) without it and 51% (0.77) with the AORC rain to midnight: the gain comes from the hours after about 09:00, not from the product.

Rain up to the evening of the issue day closes about a quarter of the gap in onsets warned: 19% to 30%, where the upper bound is 64%, in every seed; its NSE result is mixed: the median rises from 0.59 to 0.67, but the NSE is higher in only 5 of 12 basins.

Rain up to midnight (AORC) closes 71% of that gap in onsets warned (19% to 51%) and 65% of the gap in NSE (0.59 to 0.77, where the upper bound is 0.86): by the rule of section 4.2 the gains in onsets and in NSE are both a clear gain (the NSE is higher in 10 of 12 basins). Its single seeds span 49% to 55% of the onsets and 0.70 to 0.77 NSE.

Gains of the LSTM over past weather + river gauge, 1 day ahead (the length of the bars; differences taken before rounding): the river gauge itself adds +0.15 NSE and +1 percentage point of onsets warned to past weather only (no clear change in the onsets: seed by seed -1 to +2); rain up to the evening +0.08 and +11; rain up to midnight (AORC) +0.18 and +33; the perfect weather forecast, an upper bound, +0.28 and +46. Beyond the NLDAS rain up to the evening the AORC rain adds +0.09 and +21; what is left to the upper bound beyond the AORC rain is +0.10 and +13.

The sets are alternatives, not a chain: each reads past weather + river gauge plus its own input. The AORC network does not read the NLDAS rain, and the perfect weather forecast reads the weather recorded for the three coming days (all of it, with the rain that fell after the morning of the issue day, which the rain table stamps on the next day: an inference from the project's own data, section 4.5 of the report) and not the extra rain of the other sets. All bars start at the level of past weather + river gauge (the dashed line) so that their lengths compare. In the lower block the light part of a bar is the gain of the rain up to midnight and the dark part what the real forecast (or the perfect rain) adds to it, because those networks read both.

Kinds of model on the same inputs, past weather + river gauge, 1 day ahead: median NSE 0.56 (ridge regression), 0.59 (random forest), 0.59 (LSTM) and 0.58 (Transformer), 0.03 apart; onsets warned 11% (ridge regression), 18% (random forest), 19% (LSTM) and 14% (Transformer), 8 percentage points apart. Between the LSTM and the best simple model (ridge regression, chosen on the validation years) the NSE shows no clear difference: the LSTM is higher in 5 of 12 basins (p = 0.85).

With past weather only the kinds of model lie 0.11 NSE apart: 0.33 (ridge regression), 0.38 (random forest) and 0.44 (LSTM, single seeds 0.36 to 0.43). Against the best simple model (random forest) the LSTM is ahead only as the average of its three seeds: the averaged forecast is higher in 11 of 12 basins, but the random forest lies inside the range of the single LSTM seeds, so one training alone is not clearly ahead.

Kinds of model given the new inputs (the small marks). With the AORC rain up to midnight, 1 day ahead: ridge regression warns of 55% of the onsets (67% of its warnings false) and scores a median NSE of 0.64; random forest warns of 48% of the onsets (53% of its warnings false) and scores a median NSE of 0.66; the LSTM 51% (50% false) and 0.77. The new input adds +45 points of onsets warned to ridge regression, +30 to the random forest and +33 to the LSTM, so the gain in onsets does not need the network; the simple models sit at another operating point (ridge regression more onsets and more false warnings than the LSTM, random forest fewer onsets and more false warnings than the LSTM); by the NSE and the rule of section 4.2 the LSTM is ahead against ridge regression, the LSTM is ahead against random forest. The three lie 0.13 NSE and 7 percentage points of onsets apart here, against 0.03 and 8 with past weather + river gauge. With the GEFS forecast, 2 and 3 days ahead: ridge regression warns of 59% and 52% of the onsets (60% and 61% of its warnings false) with a median NSE of 0.41 and 0.36; random forest warns of 47% and 42% of the onsets (47% and 49% of its warnings false) with a median NSE of 0.54 and 0.47; the LSTM 39% and 37% (40% and 41% false), 0.53 and 0.45. Against the random forest the LSTM shows no clear difference 2 days ahead and no clear difference 3 days ahead; both simple models warn of more onsets than the LSTM, with more of their warnings false (another operating point): the gain from the forecast does not need the network either.

What the title rests on: on the same inputs (past weather + river gauge) the four kinds of model lie closer together (0.03 NSE; 8 percentage points of onsets warned) than every gain of the LSTM over past weather + river gauge (+0.08, +0.18 and +0.28 NSE; +11, +33 and +46 points). In onsets warned the margin against the rain up to the evening is small (8 against +11): the kinds of model range from 11% to 19% (the note 'Kinds of model on the same inputs' lists them). What they share is that none of them warns of more than 19% of the onsets, where the rain up to the evening gives 30%, the AORC rain up to midnight 51% and the upper bound 64%. With past weather only the same does not hold in NSE (0.11 apart, against +0.08 for the smallest of those gains): the note 'With past weather only' says how that difference is read.

The Transformer comes from its own experiment (results/model_comparison.json): it was trained beside an LSTM twin with the same settings (sequences of 365 days, at most 1,000 updates, two seeds each), not beside the LSTM drawn with past weather + river gauge. It is drawn at its own scores (median NSE 0.58, 14% of onsets warned) beside that LSTM, not shifted or rescaled; its LSTM twin scores 0.60 and 18%, the LSTM drawn there 0.59 and 19%.

With the rain up to the evening and with the perfect weather forecast (the upper bound) only the LSTM is drawn. No other kind of model was run with the rain up to the evening; with the perfect weather forecast the LSTM and the simple models do not read the same days of weather 1 day ahead (the LSTM reads the weather of all three coming days, the simple models only up to the day being forecast), so no comparison is like-for-like there and no winner is called.
'Tomorrow = today' reads the river gauge only: median NSE 0.43, and 0% of the onsets warned, because its forecast is above the high-flow level only when the river already is.

GO, by criteria fixed before the analysis: at least 70% warned and at most 30% false warnings. The figure draws the first half (the green band). For onsets at the high-flow level itself, 1 day ahead: past weather + river gauge 19% warned, 59% false (NOT YET); rain up to the evening 30% and 63% (NOT YET); AORC rain up to midnight 51% and 50% (NOT YET); the upper bound 64% and 26% (CAUTION).

Verdicts for onsets, by the criteria of results/flood_analysis.json, at the fixed warning level of the figure and at the level chosen on the validation years (as the results files store it): NOT YET for every set that could be had in practice, at both levels and at every lead time drawn (21 sets and models counted). The upper bounds: perfect weather forecast 1 day ahead CAUTION; perfect rain of the three days 2 days ahead CAUTION; perfect weather forecast 2 days ahead CAUTION (GO at the chosen level); perfect rain of the three days 3 days ahead CAUTION; perfect weather forecast 3 days ahead CAUTION. The perfect rain of the three days warns of 71% of the onsets 3 days ahead with 30.03% of its warnings false: CAUTION, 0.03 points of false warnings short of GO.

The lower block, 2 and 3 days ahead (results/forecast_input.json): the real weather forecast is the control member of the GEFSv12 reforecast, rain only, for the three days being forecast, from the 00 UTC run of the UTC date t+1 (the latest run that exists at the issue time), averaged over each basin and bias-corrected per basin on the validation years; it is put in place of the AORC rain of those days (an analysis made after the fact) that the networks of the AORC set were trained on (a substitution, not a retraining). It adds +18 and +25 points of onsets warned to the rain up to midnight (21% and 12% to 39% and 37%; clear in every training) and +0.15 and +0.20 NSE (mixed by the rule of section 4.2: higher in 8 and 9 of 12 basins); counted from the rain table alone, +30 and +31 points and +0.21 and +0.20 NSE (the bars). It closes 37% and 42% of the gap in onsets warned from the rain up to midnight to the perfect rain. One member only, 0.25-degree cells over basins of 112 to 1,927 km2, one bias factor per basin: a measurement of what such a forecast is worth, not of what a service would deliver (in Eastern summer the last files of the run are posted up to 15 minutes after the issue time, a margin measured on four days of the operational archive).

1 day ahead the same forecast, substituted in the same way, warns of 45% of the onsets against 51% without it at the fixed warning level, with 35% of its warnings false against 50%: fewer onsets and fewer false warnings, a moved operating point, which the independent review of that experiment (results/review_forecast_input.json) does not read as lost skill; it is not drawn. The experiment's own shuffled-forecast control is not a neutral baseline (a network trained on the AORC rain and given noise collapses), so it is not drawn either. Retrained with the forecast as an input on a shorter split (train 2000-2008, test 2010-2014, with 335, 540, 656 onsets at 1, 2 and 3 days; its own scores, not comparable in level with the figure) the onsets warned go from 41%, 14%, 8% to 61%, 49%, 44% (perfect rain 72%, 77%, 77%); that retrained result is left to the report and is not drawn.

Not drawn, and where to find it: the ERA5 rain to midnight (E1: 30% of the onsets, median NSE 0.66, the same share as the NLDAS rain up to the evening, a stand-in for AORC with the right clock; the report section on it) and the 63 training rivers instead of 12 (E3: for the same 12 rivers 1 day ahead median NSE 0.59 to 0.60, onsets warned 19% to 17% with 50% of the warnings false: no clear difference in NSE; more rivers are not more information about the day).

The renderings: report = the drawing with its own title, subtitle and footnote; plain = the same drawing without them and without the rows 'river gauge only' and 'past weather only' (page 1 of the report); talk = for the closing slide, at larger lettering, without the rows 'river gauge only', 'past weather only' and 'perfect rain', without the small marks except at past weather + river gauge, without the control and the lines of the single seeds (none of them is in the headline); the numbers it draws are the same.

The LSTM mark is the forecast averaged over its seeds (3, 3, 3, 3, 3 seeds, from top to bottom of the upper block); the thin line with caps is the range of the single seeds. The averaged forecast can score above every single seed.
Among the models tried: 'tomorrow = today', ridge regression, random forest, an LSTM with 64 memory cells and a small Transformer. Larger networks were not tried.

The same quantities 2 and 3 days ahead for the sets of the upper block (including the ones the lower block does not draw) are under 'not_drawn' (l2, l3), with the same keys as 'levels', 'steps' and 'control'; 'far' holds the five sets of the lower block, with their gains over the rain table + river gauge and the forecast's own part.
Every number of the figure is read from a results file ('sources' names the file and the key); 1039 values that a second file or key also holds were compared and all agree (largest difference 6e-17).

figure.footnote: Test years 2005-2014, 12 basins. Onset: a high-flow day forecast while the river was still below the high-flow level. Bars start at past weather + river gauge. Hatched: an upper bound that cannot be had in practice. AORC: an analysis made after the fact; diamonds: Stage IV radar, a real-time product, in its place (right), without its last hour (left). GEFS: archived forecast rain of the next three days, one member, put in place of the AORC rain of those days that the model was trained on; lower block, light part of a bar: the rain up to midnight, dark part: what the forecast adds. Control: the same rain one day older. figure.asterisk: * The Transformer comes from its own experiment (its LSTM twin: 18% of onsets warned, median NSE 0.60).
panel_titles: Median NSE of the 12 basins (1 = perfect)
how_to_read: One row per set of information, from the least (top) to the most (bottom). Left panel: the share of onsets warned (the green band is what GO asks for); right panel: the median NSE of the basins. The upper block is 1 day ahead; the lower block is two and three days ahead, one pair of narrow panels for each lead time.

Large blue dot: the LSTM, the forecast averaged over its seeds; thin black line with caps behind it: the range of its single seeds (hidden where they lie inside the dot); bold numbers: the value of the dot.

Thick bar: from the level of past weather + river gauge (the dashed vertical line) to the dot, so its length is what the extra information gives. In the lower block the light part of a bar is the gain of the rain up to midnight and the dark part what the real forecast, or the perfect rain, adds to it.
Hatched row, dashed bar, light dot: a perfect weather forecast, an upper bound that cannot be had in practice.

Small hollow circle under the rain up to the evening: the control of the rain-timing experiment, the same rain one day older. Two hollow diamonds under the AORC rain: the real-time check, the same networks given Stage IV radar rain in place of AORC on the issue day (right) and with its last hour left out (left).

Small coloured marks: the other kinds of model, drawn only where they read the same information as the LSTM - 'tomorrow = today' (grey diamond) with the river gauge only, ridge regression (triangle) and random forest (square) with past weather only, with past weather + river gauge, with the AORC rain up to midnight (1 day ahead) and with the GEFS forecast (2 and 3 days ahead), the Transformer (star, from its own experiment) with past weather + river gauge.
Bracket at past weather + river gauge, with the note beside it: from the lowest to the highest of the kinds of model on the same inputs.
'mixed' beside an NSE value: the gain over past weather + river gauge is a mixed result by the rule of section 4.2 (the median rises, but not clearly).
figure.caption: What to see: on the same inputs (past weather + river gauge) the four kinds of model lie within 0.03 NSE and 8 percentage points of each other; the gains of the LSTM from more information are larger (+11, +33 and +46 points of onsets warned with the rain up to the evening, the AORC rain up to midnight and a perfect weather forecast, an upper bound that cannot be had in practice). AORC is an analysis made after the fact; with Stage IV radar in its place 48% of the onsets are warned. 2 and 3 days ahead a real weather forecast lifts the onsets warned from 8% and 6% to 39% and 37%. The NSE gain with rain up to the evening (+0.08) is a mixed result: higher in only 5 of 12 basins. For onsets the verdict is NOT YET for every set that could be had in practice.
figure.caption_words_the_plain_figure_does_not_: Bars start at the dashed line, the level of past weather + river gauge; in the lower block (two and three days ahead, 951 and 1,116 onsets) the light part of a bar is the gain of the rain up to midnight and the dark part what the forecast, or the perfect rain, adds to it. AORC is an analysis made after the fact; the hollow diamonds are the same networks given Stage IV radar rain, a real-time product, in its place on the issue day (48% of the onsets warned) and with its last hour left out (45%). GEFS: archived forecast rain of the next three days, one member, put in place of the AORC rain of those days that the model was trained on. 'mixed' beside an NSE value: the gain over past weather + river gauge is a mixed result. Small marks are drawn also with the AORC rain (1 day) and with the GEFS forecast (2 and 3 days): at the fixed warning level they sit at another operating point, with more of their warnings false than the LSTM's.
